subject: chickenWalker
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: chicken-legged walking house-machine.
Style: Howl's Moving Castle.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a ramshackle, steampunk patchwork house walking on giant chicken legs, Howl's Moving Castle meets Baba Yaga's hut, aiming for 180-340 richly textured parts within roughly 700-900 lines, making sure it's correct against the SDK without the ability to test it live.

Each leg needs a thigh, shin, three forward toes plus a back toe with talons, and feathery "pants" around the upper legs. The body should layer a main hall, a tower with a pointed roof, a smoking chimney, balconies, glowing windows, a round door, and scrappy add-ons like a copper dome, pipes, boiler tank, gear train, lanterns, flags, chains, and laundry lines -- and I want to give it a bit of character with a beak-shaped front porch awning flanked by round "eye" windows.

Now I'm working out the rig: treating it like a creature built skeleton-first, with a root hull, hip joints, knees, ankles/hocks, and toes, using IK for the legs. I'm setting proportions so the whole thing stands around 8 meters tall -- legs roughly 3.2m with hips near y=3.3, and a house body about 4m wide sitting on top, with coordinates oriented so the front of the house (with door, porch, and beak awning) faces +Z, and I'm sketching the digitigrade leg chain as hip-to-knee-forward, knee-to-hock-back, then toes, using segment lengths around 1.3m and 1.5m.

I'm checking that the hip-to-target distance is reachable given the summed leg segment lengths, and defining the bend directions so the knee points forward and the hock points backward, naming the joint chain hipL, kneeL, hockL, ankleL for the left leg's four points across three segments.

Now I'm working out how to sweep the limb as a polyline chain with a radius function varying by position, so the thigh reads thicker than the shin and tarsus.

Feathered thigh transitioning into scaly yellow tarsus near the bottom—coloring by bands with feathers covering the upper leg and yellow scales taking over near the foot.

I'm also considering adding a riveted iron collar as a hip joint where the leg attaches to the house. For the toes, I'm planning three front toes plus a back hallux, each built from two segments ending in a talon spike, with the toe bases positioned so the foot rests correctly on the floor.

Still refining toe geometry...

I'm thinking about adding ridged scutes along the toes and a rooster-style spur at the back of the tarsus for extra detail. For the house base, I'm planning a chunky timber-and-iron platform sitting around y 3.2–3.6 where the legs socket into the underside.

Now I'm designing the main house as a Howl-like ramshackle structure made of several volumes, starting with a rounded iron-plated hull platform shaped with a lofted profile that narrows into a beak-like prow at the front, using varying width and height stations from back to front.

For the main hall, I'm planning a box with wood plank walls and timber framing, glowing windows, and a crooked gable roof extruded from a triangular outline, with patchwork tile textures made from striped rows of terracotta and teal paint to mimic Howl's castle style.

Actually I'm reconsidering the roof construction: instead of a single extruded shape, I'll build it from two tilted slab panels with eave overhangs plus wooden gable triangles, using a patches() texture with rust red, teal, ochre, and slate colors for that patchwork tile look.

I'm setting the extrude direction and thickness so the shape centers correctly, then planning a tall round tower with a conical roof, round glowing windows, and a balcony ring, with a slight rotation to give it a leaning, crooked look.

Next I'm sketching a smaller gable annex on the opposite side, oriented sideways with a patched blue roof, positioning its box dimensions to tuck against the main hall.

For the base, I want a wide platform (around 5.4 units) with legs spaced further apart near the center, giving that classic top-heavy Baba Yaga hut silhouette. Behind the house I'll add a copper boiler tank with verdigris, plumbing pipes, a tall smoking chimney, and maybe a playful tail-feather fan detail on the back for character.

Thinking through that tail feature more, I'm picturing a rooster-style tail made of 7-9 long curved feather blades in teal, green, and orange, fanning out behind the house as a signature flourish, built using extruded feather shapes with a center rachis and gradient coloring, angled outward and tilted back for a dynamic fan effect.

Working out the cross product so the thickness axis aligns with z, then sketching an asymmetric curved leaf outline to give the sickle feather its characteristic curl.

I'll paint the feather with a gradient from orange root to green to teal tip, plus a peacock-style eye spot near the end using distance-based coloring, and a pale quill stripe down the center. Given the hut is only about 5m wide, I should scale the feather down to roughly 2.4m length so it stays proportional.

For the tail, I'll settle on 7 feathers around 2.6m long, anchored at the back of the platform and angled upward and backward like a dangling flamboyant plume in Howl's Moving Castle style. I might also add a red rooster comb along the roof ridge to reinforce the chicken-legged house theme.

For the front entrance, I'm turning the porch into a beak: an upper beak formed as a forward-pointing extruded wedge awning, and a lower beak acting as a hinged jaw that doubles as a drawbridge ramp/staircase leading to the door, complete with chains for lowering it.

I also want to give the castle a face — two large round glowing windows styled like chicken eyes (orange iris, black pupil, white highlight, with shutter lids) placed on the front gable on either side of the beak-porch, like Howl's Moving Castle's expressive facade.

I'm laying out the front elevation coordinates: the main hall front wall, eye-window positions and radii, and the beak structure protruding forward between them, with the lower beak forming a ramp-like extension below.

I'm adjusting the ramp to a gentler 20° downward tilt so it doesn't look like a stairway to nowhere, and now sketching the upper beak as a forward-pointing wedge defined by a side-view profile.

Trying a flattened cone shape for the beak instead, scaling it along the depth axis so it tapers correctly when oriented along the z-axis.

Positioning the beak cone at the wall so its base embeds flush, with the apex pointing outward along the forward direction. I'm thinking about adding small nostril ellipsoids, but the beak base now overlaps the door opening, so I need to raise the hall wall height to around 2.6 units tall to clear the conflict.

I'm reworking the vertical placement: door spans roughly y 3.65–4.5, beak sits a bit higher around y 5.0, and eyes flank the beak at x ±1.05–1.15, checking the radii so nothing visually collides within the hall's half-width of 1.8. Now I'm sketching the door itself as an arched wooden design with plank textures, hinges, and a small glowing window to sit beneath the beak on a porch deck.

Designing window and wall textures...

Setting up the bone hierarchy next: a root "hull" joint at the body center with a spine role, then additional joints for the tower, chimney, jaw, and tail base so feather or fan parts can attach to them.

I'll keep the tail as a single joint, skip hinging the door separately, and add a fun small detail — a spinning weathervane joint with a rooster cutout on the chimney pole. Also planning the vehicle name label and the neutral rest pose for the legs.

Now sketching the set of wow textures: a feather tuft card, a glowing chicken eye, door and warm-glow window svgs, a porthole variant for the tower, a cloth pennant banner with a stitched rooster/sun emblem, a string of bunting flags, a chimney smoke puff cloud, and a sign texture still being defined.

I'll settle on a hanging wooden sign reading "THE ROOST" rendered with serif text. I'm also planning a clockwork gauge texture for the boiler along with a steampunk gear train on the hull side, using metal paints, panelled hull texture, and coil details, importing from the clockwork kit path.

Beyond that, I'm layering in roof patchwork and mossy noise paint, skipping mushrooms, and adding glow sources like lantern lights, lit windows, glowing eyes, chimney embers, and boiler vents. For the overall palette I'm channeling a Howl's Moving Castle feel — muted, painterly tones of weathered wood, slate, rust, teal copper, ochre, cream plaster, dark iron, and warm feather oranges and greens.

Now I'm setting up the imports from the agentic-3js-builder SDK, pulling in geometry helpers, painting/texture utilities, and the glow and clockwork kits, then initializing the builder for an 8-meter hen house model with a large paint texture size.

I need a part-creation helper, but I'm worried about bone resolution — since joints exist at the hull and hips are close together, nearby house parts might accidentally attach to the wrong joint. I'll explicitly pass the hull bone for all house parts to avoid misattachment.

I'll just use a loose `any` type for the options to avoid fighting the type system, then move on to defining the actual coordinate constants for each section.

Now I'm working out the hull geometry: placing the hip joint and platform near y=3.4, figuring out where the legs emerge relative to the platform's bottom edge, then setting the hull/hall section's vertical range above the platform top.

Then I'm positioning the door, beak, and eyes within the hall's front face, before working up through the roof's gable dimensions, ridge height, comb, tower, and chimney to total around 10m tall. I'm checking that this scale feels proportionate for a walking house inspired by Baba Yaga's hut, settling on a sizable but believable structure.

Now I'm laying out the main hall's footprint and the platform beneath it, defining loft stations along the depth to shape a wide, prow-like hull with a straight centerline, keeping the cross-section boxy for a clean panelled look while leaving room for legs and upper annex details.

I also want to add a walkway balcony around the platform edges with railings made of posts and rods, spacing roughly a dozen posts per side along the porch and hall boundary.

To keep the part count manageable, I'm building a small bucket helper that collects geometries by color and merges them into a single mesh before attaching to a bone, using indexed box/cylinder/sphere geometries with consistent attributes and the BufferGeometryUtils merge function.

Now I'm shaping the roof: extruding a slightly crooked peaked outline along the depth axis with overhangs, sketching out triangle-ish vertex coordinates for the main roof silhouette.

I'm simplifying the roof to a sharp triangular gable, positioned slightly forward of the hall's front wall to create an overhang, and considering adding a round attic window on the gable face as a decorative third "eye" above the wall beneath it.

Writing crest outline coordinates...

I'm shading the comb with a red gradient, lighter toward the top. For wattles, I'm hanging small red teardrop lobes below the lower beak at the front of the platform instead of near the door, so they don't block the entrance.

Actually, I'll turn those wattles into a pair of glowing red paper lanterns hanging from the porch's bottom edge, Howl-style, which doubles as decorative lighting. For the roofline, I'm planning a circular tower on the left side and a lean-to annex roof on the right, working out their placement along the x-axis relative to the platform edges.

Positioning the tower at the back corner so it overlaps the hall corner slightly, with a leaning conical roof that pokes through the main roofline for that ramshackle charm. I'll build it as a tapered lathe shape, defining the base-to-top profile with a slight axis tilt.

Writing lathe profile points...

Finishing the lathe outline closing back to the axis, then placing the roof paint and tower top position. I'm also working out window portholes on the tower surface using decals positioned by angle around the cylinder.

Now I'm sizing the annex structure, letting it overhang the platform edge slightly for a corbelled look, and sketching its gable roof outline with a ridge running along the z-axis.

For the chimney, I'm planning a tall brick stack through the main roof near the back-left, giving it a square cross-section with a cap and smoke effect, plus a separate iron pipe stack with an elbow for the boiler. I'm working out a brick-texture paint function using offset row patterns based on position.

Writing brick paint function...

For the smoke, I'm considering low-poly icosahedron spheres as rising puffs instead of flat cards, since they'd give a more three-dimensional cloud-like look leaning back from the chimney top.

Now I'm placing a horizontal boiler tank cylinder at the back of the platform, figuring out its radius and position so it rests properly resting on the platform surface, with a copper verdigris material.

I'm adding domed end caps using squashed spheres, bands and rivets along the boiler surface, a pressure gauge and valve, a pipe leading into the chimney tower, and tail feathers positioned behind and above the boiler fanning out from their base point.

Switching to a lathe-based boiler profile with a defined radius/axis outline, painted in copper verdigris with sharp creased corners. Adding torus bands wrapped around the boiler axis for the metal straps.

For the pressure gauge placement, I'm deciding to mount it on the boiler's end cap facing the left side, since the back face toward the hall wall would be hidden from view.

Next I'm positioning a brass bezel cylinder angled at 45 degrees on the top-back of the boiler, then moving on to plan the gear train assembly on the platform's side wall, figuring out where the gears fit given the tapering wall width.

I'm sizing the gears with module-based teeth counts, realizing the larger gear will overhang the platform and hang down near the leg, which actually adds nice steampunk flavor. I'm planning to mirror this with a second gear train on the opposite side using a reusable helper function with joint-based gear spin names.

Now I'm adding hip collar details—torus rings bolted at the thigh tops like iron flanges—and sketching out thigh surface decorations like scattered feather cards.

For the leg sweep itself, I'm building a single band-based sweep from the chain so plumage transitions into scale material partway down, then scattering feather cards only on the upper plumage region above the hock, filtering hits by their y-position relative to that joint point.

Trying to pin down exactly where the hock sits numerically — computing segment lengths against the root-to-target distance to figure out how the leg bends, since the last segment runs straight down parallel to the overall limb direction.

Solving the triangle gives knee position roughly 0.665 down and 1.117 forward from the hip, which matches the real chicken anatomy where the thigh angles forward and the knee sits hidden in the body feathers before the shin bends back toward a vertical tarsus. I'm working out the bend direction for the hock using the plane defined by root, target, and the bend hint, treating it as lying in the yz-plane.

I'll avoid hard-coding assumptions and instead derive positions from the computed points directly, checking that the knee stays safely under the platform front and that the shin/hock geometry stays clear of the ramp. For the feather culling, I'm comparing heights against the hock level to decide which segments get hidden versus visible, and adjusting leg segment lengths to get a more convincing chicken silhouette.

For card feathers I'm setting size and lean angles with a downward flow direction so they wrap the leg naturally, using cross-facing cards so they read from any viewing angle, applying this to both legs symmetrically.

For pants texture I'm drawing overlapping feather clusters in orange and cream with dark outlines, then adding a hock bulge using a sphere to simulate the knee joint, computing radius tapering along the leg chain based on segment length ratios.

The leg radius shrinks smoothly from thigh through knee to shin, hits a slight bulge at the hock, then quickly narrows into the scaly tarsus and toes, with a hard color seam separating feathered plumage from scaled skin.

I'm leaning into speckled hen plumage—warm brown with mottled countershading—paired with ochre-yellow scaled legs, deciding against literal bird-black to keep the Howl aesthetic. Now I'm laying out the toe structure: three front toes splayed at angles with varying lengths, plus a shorter rear toe, building the joint chain from ankle outward.

Still working out toe joint positions and naming...

Still writing sweep geometry...

Still placing the rear spur...

Now I'm setting up leg joint chains with side-based naming, and planning the tail joint and feather placement using an extrude operation off the tail bone.

For the tail feather coloring, I'm defining a gradient paint that shifts from orange-brown through green to teal along the feather length, with a cream quill down the center, subtle angled barb stripes, and an eye spot near the tip.

I'm also working out how to vary feather lengths across the tail by generating a scaled outline per length and baking separate paint closures for each variant rather than trying to share a single uniform scale.

For the fan arrangement, I'm spacing nine feathers across the angle range with lengths decreasing toward the edges, tilting them all slightly backward in z, and computing each feather's direction vector so the fan spreads outward in x while staying anchored properly at the extremes.

Checking geometry, the outer feathers rise around 30° and splay out in x without hitting the tower or hall roof since they're positioned well behind those structures. Now I'm planning the weathervane: a pole on the tower roof topped with a rooster silhouette, which I'll construct as a simple extruded profile from roughly twenty outline points.

Plotting rooster silhouette points...

Still tracing the path coordinates, checking whether any of these segments around the neck and tail cross each other before closing the loop back to the starting point.

Then I'm positioning the weathervane: setting up its extrusion with a thin profile, orienting it so the rooster faces forward, and planning its placement joint at the tower's top, just above the roof cone's tip.

That brings the total structure to around 12 meters, which feels too tall for the scale I want. I'm scaling down the tower height so the body, roof, ridge, comb, and chimney all shrink proportionally, landing the total around 10.5 meters — a more reasonable size while still matching the dramatic feel of Howl's castle.

Checking the tower's position against the boiler and annex, I realize they overlap in x-range near the base, so I need to shift the boiler further left to clear the tower's platform edge.

Checking the feather root position against the boiler back clears fine at z=-2.85. I'm thinking of adding a tail mount bracket where the platform meets the tail, plus a small brass hub disc where the feathers converge. Now I'm considering the chimney placement, deciding whether it should pierce the roof on the left side near the hall.

Checking clearance against the roof's back eave at z -1.95, the pipe at z -2.2 stays clear, so I'm plotting a curved path with a slight tilted elbow near the top for a jaunty look.

Working out ring placement along the pipe...

Now I'm thinking about adding bunting between the tower and roof — a sagging rope with flag cards hanging off it, using frames along the rope path that face outward and upward so each flag card orients correctly.

Working out the card orientation: since lean:180 flips the card downward, I need to draw the triangle with its wide base at the drawing's bottom edge so that once hung, the base appears at the top and the tip hangs down. Now I'm figuring out where the flag line actually stretches between — from the tower's midpoint toward the front of the hall.

For the bunting rope itself, I'm checking a path from the chimney cap to the tower, making sure it sags enough to clear the roof ridge and the comb detail without clipping through them, nudging the rope height higher where it crosses near the ridge.

Now I'm thinking about adding one more bunting strand, maybe from the annex ridge to the platform's front rail post, then stopping there. For the lanterns, I want a Howl's-Moving-Castle-style hanging lamp made from a sphere with a soft glow, and I'm figuring out placement.

I'll put two red lanterns flanking the porch beak on small bracket arms, one on the tower balcony, and more hanging from the platform's front corners, plus iron lamp posts at the deck corners. For a signboard, I'm hanging a wooden plank reading "THE ROOST" from a bracket arm on the annex's front wall, using a textured plane for the wood-and-text look.

For the backing, I'm layering a thin wood slab box behind the sign's front plane for depth. Now I'm designing a reusable window function that builds a wood frame around a glowing plane, and figuring out placement on the hall's side walls, working around where the tower and annex roofline interrupt the surface.

Reworking the annex's footprint slightly so a window can sit cleanly past its edge, I'm also sketching the window texture itself—an amber-gradient pane with dark mullions and a sill, plus optional teal shutter boxes flanking it. Then I'm planning matching windows for the annex's front and end walls.

Now I'm adding round window decals to the tower cylinder, and reworking the loft platform into a tapered deck with planked texture—defining width stations at several z-positions (3.4, 5.0, 5.6, 5.2, 2.4 wide) that interpolate linearly between them to shape the porch's narrowing silhouette.

For the surface treatment, I'm deciding that flat top faces (n.y>0.7) get a wooden deck plank texture while other surfaces get panelled iron, nesting a custom paint function inside the hull paint logic to switch between the two looks.

Now I'm working out the beak geometry: an upper beak cone and the lower beak as a tapering wedge-shaped jaw built from loft stations, which I'll pose onto a jaw bone with rotation around the x-axis.

I'm thinking about chains sweeping from the ramp tip to the lamp post as sagging catenary rods, but since rods ride rigidly on bones, I realize the chain geometry needs to be built after posing the jaw, using the local point derived post-pose rather than trying to inherit bone transforms directly.

Rather than posing the jaw after building it, I realize I can just construct the ramp already inclined in its final open position, setting the joint's rest direction along the rotated vector directly. The jaw joint connects to the hull at the hinge point aimed along that direction, so the rest pose is naturally the open mouth shape with upper and lower jaw built as separate pieces. Then I move to building the ramp geometry as a loft from the hinge to the tip point.

For the cleats across the ramp, I'm working out orientation so each box aligns its height axis along the ramp's tangent direction rather than the hinge direction, trying to figure out the right frame for placing them evenly along the inclined path.

Placing geometry along direction vectors...

For the eyes, I'm planning textured circle planes facing forward with a glowing texture, surrounded by a round metallic rim built from a torus ring.

Building droopy eyelid shapes...

For a sleepy-friendly lid shape, I'm thinking of tilting the eyelid shape by adjusting the extrude axes slightly instead of changing the arc geometry directly, so the chord slants without creating a self-intersecting polygon.

Now I'm working out the eye and beak placement relative to the wall: eyes sit at x=±1.1 with radius .42, leaving the beak half-width around 0.62. I'm also checking that the door arch below the beak clears the beak's lowest point and fits proportionally against the door's width and height.

Realizing a 1m door is too small for human scale—I need roughly 1m×2m—which means raising the overall hall height to about 2.8m (from y=3.7 to 6.5) so the beak and a proper-sized door can both fit above the doorway without clashing.

I'm reconsidering placement entirely: maybe the door shouldn't be on the symmetric front face with the eyes and beak at all, but instead on a side wall near the porch walkway, keeping the front purely as the "face" with a small hatch under the beak, while the ramp leads around to the actual entrance.

Actually the legs look too short for a proper Howl's castle feel, so I'm lengthening them and shifting the platform height up, then working out parameters: platform top, hip position, and leg lengths that sum correctly to reach the ankles, plus the hall width.

Working out the beak, eye, and window placements relative to the hall height, making sure eyes and beak lids fit between the door arch and the roof eave without overlapping, then positioning side windows at a lower floor level before moving on to the roof dimensions.

Now I'm sketching the roof geometry—the triangular outline, its overhang relative to the gable face, and a round attic window glowing near the ridge comb—then shifting to defining the annex structure's position, dimensions, and its own peaked roof offset from the main hall.

The annex roof, pitched at 1.9 wide, actually overlaps into the hall wall by a small margin, which I decide is fine structurally. Checking the platform width against the annex's slight overhang, I plan corbel braces to support it, then move to laying out the tower's base height, hat height, and vane position, noting the total height feels a bit tall but acceptable for now.

Reconsidering proportions, I lower the tower height (TH=4.2, hat 2.2, vane 11.6) so it reads as a tall skinny castle silhouette with varied rooflines—tower roof peeking above the hall ridge. For the chimney, I shorten it to about 1.8 tall and work out where its base needs to sit so it's properly embedded into the sloped roof surface near x=-0.9, checking the roof's height at that slope to ensure the chimney box bottom doesn't float above the surface.

Then I move on to the boiler and tail feather placement, and start sketching a tower balcony: a thin lathe disc for the platform plus a railing, though I realize the disc radius needs to clear the tower's own solid radius so it doesn't intersect and look broken.

For the railing I decide to use a bucket of posts placed at computed angles around the balcony, with a torus ring merged in for the top rail, which feels simpler than trying to use a repeating ring helper directly. I leave the balcony access and door question unresolved for now and move on to hall front wall details like iron straps and patched planks.

For the patchwork wall look, I'm defining a plank color palette and writing a paint function that computes row and fractional position from y, picks a sampling axis based on normal direction, and uses cell-based coloring to scatter patch regions...

Still writing styles...

Setting plank rows at 0.3m with 2.5cm seams keeps within the 0.09 fraction threshold, and the 2048 paint sheet is sufficient. Now I'm budgeting the flat color count, aiming for a palette of roughly 30 named colors like iron dark, wood tones, rust, and teal, making sure textures and paints don't count against that limit.

I'm expanding the palette with more named hex values—teal dark, ochre, cream, reds, yellows, oranges, lantern orange, brass, smoke tones, navy, and a warm glass color—while noting that textured parts still need a white base color for proper tinting. Now I'm starting a helper function to construct the lantern piece.

Writing lantern geometry...

Plates will use steel/blued/copper materials with bucket-sphere nails at corners. For timber framing, I'll add corner posts and middle belts as wood boxes, plus rotated boxes for diagonal braces on the side walls, tilting them in the y-z plane to simulate angled bracing.

Setting up the Bucket helper class to merge geometries by color...

I need to watch out for mergeGeometries failing on non-indexed shapes like icosahedrons -- those need normalization before merging alongside indexed geometries like boxes and cylinders.

Writing feather tuft SVG...

For the eye, I'm planning a circular iris disc with amber coloring, a dark pupil ring, and a highlight for depth.

Then for the door, I'm sketching an arched design with vertical planks, iron straps, a ring handle, and a small glowing porthole window, plus a wooden arch frame set against the solid wall behind it.

Now I'm working out the geometry so the door plane and chicken's beak don't overlap, nudging their vertical positions and radii until the layout fits cleanly.

Next I'm planning the other SVG assets: a glowing square window with frame, mullion cross, and sill (plus a round porthole variant), a wooden sign reading "THE ROOST," and a swallowtail pennant flag with a rooster or sun emblem for the tower's roof vane.

I want the card to lie in a vertical plane containing the backward axis and the width direction, with its face pointing sideways along +x so it reads properly when viewed from that side, meaning the flow direction should be set to [1,0,0] to get the normal oriented that way.

Setting up the banner frame now, with the drawing's hoist at the bottom and the swallowtail point extending upward, rotating the emblem 90 degrees so it still reads fine inside that layout, then adding a bend of 25 for proportion.

Smoke and gear textures aren't needed since those surfaces stay solid, but I'll add bunting flags as three-colored SVG triangles and a gauge using the gauge texture. For the laundry detail, I'm planning a clothesline strung along the back right with small hanging items -- a shirt, a sock, a sheet -- drawn as separate SVGs attached along a rope with a 180 lean.

Figuring out where to anchor the rope is trickier: I'm checking coordinates between the annex roof and the boiler pipe, trying to route it so it clears the tower surface and doesn't visually collide with the tail feathers, which start further back. Settling on a rope running roughly along y 7.0 near z -2.25, connecting a point near the pipe to a point near the tower's side.

I'm also tallying up the laundry items and texture count to make sure the atlas stays within a reasonable budget, landing around 14 textures which should be fine. Now I'm ready to start writing the actual code carefully.

Writing imports and setup...

Still writing brick pattern logic...

For the roof, I'm darkening near the top with a height-based gradient, then layering a patchwork paint of varied colors as roof patches, with tile rows overlaid on top using a slope-direction parameter.

Writing roof tile shading logic...

Generalizing the roof paint into a reusable function that takes a column angle function, so I can apply it to both gable and conical tower roofs. I'm also sketching out stone texture paint, reusing the hull paint scheme, and starting on deck board paint running along the z-axis.

Writing deck plank code... Then I'm defining the hull paint to switch between deck boards on top surfaces and tarnished iron panels elsewhere, and starting on a scaled texture paint for Tarsus.

Now I'm working out plumage: mottled feather coloring with small cream spots layered on top, then adding a countershading effect so the top is lighter than the underside.

Defining beak, comb, and leg materials...

Still writing barb shading...

I decide to keep the leaf flat and symmetric rather than adding sickle curvature, building the outline points as a typed tuple array for the extrude call, making sure points don't repeat and the extrude parameters include direction, y-displacement, thickness, and smoothing.

For the comb shape, I'm checking that the outline doesn't self-intersect by walking through each lobe's coordinates along the x-axis, marking sharp corners at the tip and root so smoothing handles them correctly, then closing the shape with a straight bottom edge before setting its extrusion thickness.

For the weathervane rooster, I'm confirming the orientation vectors are correct so it faces forward with the right "up" axis, then setting up the vane joint hinge on the mesh bone.

I'm verifying the leg geometry is reachable — computing the thigh and hock joint positions trigonometrically to make sure the knee lands at a sensible height and depth relative to the platform, keeping clearance between the thigh radius and the platform's underside.

Now I'm structuring the leg chain with named joints (hip, knee, hock, ankle) as a sequence of points, then sweeping it with banded radii and colors to transition from plumage to tarsus material along the limb.

Still writing radius function...

Now I'm rounding out the drumstick bulge shape and bumping the side count for smoother geometry, then scattering plumage card hits across the surface to place tuft textures.

I'm positioning the hip flange as a torus collar at the platform underside, then moving to the toe geometry: computing three toe directions with yaw offsets spreading left, center, and right from the ankle joint, using sine/cosine to splay them outward.

Writing toe mesh code...

Adding rear toe claws...

Then I'm placing the ankle knob as a small sphere bone part and a spur on the tarsus joint, keeping toe angles mirrored symmetrically across sides. Now I'm setting up the joint creation order, starting with the root hull joint.

Still defining joints...

I'm adding a tower joint off the hull for sway, attaching body, roof, balcony, and window parts to it, with the vane parented to the tower too -- keeping things simple rather than over-engineering extra joints. I'm also adding gear joints parented to the hull and making sure every part lacking an explicit bone still falls back to its nearest joint.

Setting up the builder with hull as the root spine joint, then writing helper functions for boxes and a geometry bucket utility to batch-add positioned, rotated, and scaled geometries under a given bone.

Checking the merge geometries import path from the three.js addons utils module, then moving on to building the platform hull using a loft with defined positions, widths and heights.

Now I'm adding walkway rails along the platform sides with wooden posts spaced at intervals and connecting rail rods using the hull bone, plus planning a front porch rail near the ramp entrance.
